title: Implement an LRU Cache
description: Build an LRU cache from scratch — understand the doubly-linked list plus hash map trick that gives O(1) get and put.

segments.text: Today we're implementing a Least Recently Used cache. It's the most-asked data structure question in interviews, and it powers everything from CPU caches to Redis internals.
An LRU cache has a fixed capacity. When it's full and you insert a new item, you evict the least recently used one. Every access — read or write — makes that item the most recently used.

The naive approach? Use an array. On access, move the item to the front. On eviction, remove the last element. But moving an element in an array is O(n) — you have to shift everything. That's too slow.
segments.thought_prompt: What data structure lets you move an element to the front in O(1)?

segments.text: Here's the magic combo: a doubly-linked list plus a hash map. The linked list maintains access order — most recent at the head, least recent at the tail. The hash map gives O(1) key lookups to any node.
On a GET: hash map finds the node in O(1). Unlink it from its current position — O(1) because doubly-linked. Move it to the head — O(1). Return the value. Total: O(1). Beautiful.
On a PUT with a new key: create a new node, add it to the head of the list, insert the key-to-node mapping in the hash map. If we're under capacity, we're done. Simple.
But if the cache is full? Remove the tail node — that's the least recently used item. Delete its entry from the hash map. Then insert the new node at the head. Eviction is O(1) too.

Why doubly-linked and not singly-linked? When you remove a node, you need to update the previous node's next pointer. With a singly-linked list, finding the previous node is O(n). Doubly-linked gives you O(1) removal.
segments.thought_prompt: Could you use a singly-linked list if you stored prev references in the hash map instead?

segments.text: In production, multiple threads access the cache concurrently. You need locks — but a global lock kills throughput. Stripe the lock across buckets, or use a read-write lock since reads vastly outnumber writes.

Redis uses an approximated LRU — sampling random keys and evicting the oldest among them. CPU L1/L2 caches use hardware LRU variants. LinkedIn's Couchbase layer, Memcached — LRU is everywhere in production systems.

To summarize: doubly-linked list for O(1) order manipulation, hash map for O(1) lookups. Together they give you O(1) get and O(1) put. That's the LRU cache — elegant, practical, and interview-essential.
